z-m-34-01.title: Given three points, is the fourth vertex the only one?
z-m-34-01.topic: Equations of figures: the fourth vertex of a parallelogram (coordinates of points)
z-m-34-01.goal: Find by yourself, and check with coordinates, that the fourth vertex of a parallelogram with three given points can be in several places, and judge how the condition on the positions of the three points (whether they are on one line) changes the result.
z-m-34-01.material: On a coordinate plane there are three points A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(1, 3). You want to make a parallelogram whose four vertices are these three points and a point D. The vertex names were given regardless of the order in which they are connected, and the parallelogram must be a real quadrilateral whose four points are not on one line. Jiho said, "D is only (5, 4)."
z-m-34-01.thinking.0: Testing the condition under which the claim 'only one' holds
z-m-34-01.thinking.1: Setting a criterion for splitting cases and finding them without missing any
z-m-34-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the conclusion changes when the condition changes
z-m-34-01.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-01.prereq.1: Can plot points on a coordinate plane and read the change in coordinates between two points (how far across and up or down)
z-m-34-01.prereq.2: Knows the definition of a parallelogram (two pairs of opposite sides are parallel to each other)
z-m-34-01.s.s1.prompt: Is D really only one, as Jiho says? First predict how many places D could be.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.hint.0: Plot A, B, and C on a coordinate plane and, for a start, draw one parallelogram with these three points as vertices.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look for a case where D is in a different position from the first one you drew but the four points still make a parallelogram.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.o.a: 1 place: the places of A, B, C are already fixed, so the remaining point D is fixed to one too
z-m-34-01.s.s1.r.a: You already fixed the opposite points just by looking at the names A, B, C. Read again that the order of the point names was not given.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.o.b: 2 places: one above side AB and one below
z-m-34-01.s.s1.r.b: You only thought of above and below one side. Which two points are opposite each other in a parallelogram can change in three ways.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.o.c: 3 places: it depends on which of A, B, C you make the point opposite D
z-m-34-01.s.s1.r.c: You set up by yourself a criterion for splitting the cases (the point opposite D). You need to check this with actual coordinates.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.o.d: Infinitely many: wherever you put the fourth point on the plane, a parallelogram can be made
z-m-34-01.s.s1.r.d: The condition that opposite sides be parallel restricts D strongly. It can't be just anywhere.
z-m-34-01.s.s1.explain: D lands in a different place depending on whether the point opposite D is A, B, or C. Whether there really are three places you will check with coordinates in the next step.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different coordinates for D so that the four points A, B, C, D (in any order) are the four vertices of a parallelogram.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.hint.0: In the parallelogram you already drew, write how much x and y each change going from A to B, and compare whether it is the same on the opposite side.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one of A, B, C as the point opposite D, and carry the change between the other two points onto the path from D to that point.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.hint.2: After finding one, change the opposite point and repeat the same method.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The midpoints of the two segments joining the opposite points are at the same position. It makes a parallelogram.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.fail.c1: This D does not make a parallelogram. Choose one point as the point opposite D, and check whether the horizontal and vertical change between the other two points is also the same between D and that point.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.explain: D is at the three places (5, 4), (−3, 2), (3, −2). They are the cases where D is opposite C, B, and A respectively. For example, for (5, 4), the horizontal and vertical change (4, 1) from A to B is the same as the change from C to D.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Write in your own words why you can say D has only these three places.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Join the three points you found and check whether the opposite sides are parallel.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count how many of A, B, C can be chosen as the opposite point.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In my explanation, is the criterion for splitting the cases clear?
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I go on to write the reason 'there are no others'?
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.model.0: If the point opposite D is A, D is (5, 4); if B, (−3, 2); if C, (3, −2). Only A, B, C can be opposite, so those three are all.
z-m-34-01.s.s2.because.model.1: There are 3 ways to choose one of the three points as the one opposite D, and once the opposite point is fixed, D is fixed to one. So D has at most 3 places.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.prompt: This time the three points are on one line, like A(0, 0), B(2, 2), C(4, 4). What happens to a parallelogram with the four points as vertices?
z-m-34-01.s.s3.hint.0: Plot A, B, and C on a coordinate plane and check whether they are on one line.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.hint.1: Find one D using the method from before and plot the positions of the four points.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.o.a: It can't be made: the four points lie flat on one line
z-m-34-01.s.s3.o.b: It is still made in 3 places: just use the method above as it is
z-m-34-01.s.s3.r.b: If you apply the method as it is, you do get points, but you did not check whether those four points all lie on one line.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.o.c: It is made in only 1 place: the three points are in a straight line, so the cases decrease
z-m-34-01.s.s3.r.c: The issue is not that the cases decrease, but whether the quadrilateral can be made at all.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.o.d: It is made in 2 places: there is a middle point, so one on each side
z-m-34-01.s.s3.r.d: Draw where the points made from points on a straight line lie.
z-m-34-01.s.s3.explain: If the three points are on one line, the D you get by matching midpoints also lies on the same line. If all four points are on one line, the shape is flat with no area, so it is not a parallelogram. This is an example of a new condition changing the conclusion.

z-m-34-02.topic: Equations of figures: tangent lines drawn from a point outside a circle (the form of the equation of a line)
z-m-34-02.goal: First judge how many tangents there should be from a point to a circle, then find and fix the missing case (a line with no slope) in a solution that found only one.
z-m-34-02.material: There is a circle x² + y² = 9 (center at the origin, radius 3) and a point P(3, 5). Jiho tried to find the tangent lines drawn from P to the circle and solved it like this. The line numbers of the solution start from 1.
z-m-34-02.thinking.0: Checking the assumption behind the solution
z-m-34-02.thinking.1: Finding the cause when the result is different from what you expected
z-m-34-02.thinking.2: Finding the missing case yourself and checking it
z-m-34-02.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-02.prereq.1: The meaning of the distance between a point and a line
z-m-34-02.prereq.2: The meaning of the circle equation x squared plus y squared = r squared
z-m-34-02.prereq.3: The difference between lines that have a slope and lines that have none (lines parallel to the y-axis)
z-m-34-02.s.s1.prompt: Before looking at the solution, how many tangent lines can be drawn from the point P(3, 5) to this circle?
z-m-34-02.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the distance from the center of the circle to the point P with the radius and decide where P is.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.hint.1: Draw pictures for when P is on, inside, and outside the circle, and count how many tangent lines can be drawn.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.o.a: 1: only one tangent can be drawn from each point
z-m-34-02.s.s1.r.a: If the point is on the circle, there is one tangent. Check whether the point P is on, inside, or outside the circle.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.o.b: Can't tell: you need to know the distance between the point and the circle, and you don't know it now
z-m-34-02.s.s1.r.b: The distance from the origin to P can be found from the coordinates alone. It is too early to say the information is insufficient.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.o.c: 2: P is outside the circle, so one can be drawn on each side
z-m-34-02.s.s1.r.c: You predicted the number of tangents from the position of the point. This becomes the standard for comparing with the result of the solution.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.o.d: Infinitely many: some of the lines drawn from P toward the circle are always tangent
z-m-34-02.s.s1.r.d: A tangent line is a line that touches the circle at only one point. Think with a picture about how many such lines there are.
z-m-34-02.s.s1.explain: The distance from the origin to P is √34 (about 5.8), greater than the radius 3, so P is outside the circle. From a point outside a circle, 2 tangents can be drawn.
z-m-34-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose one line in Jiho's solution that has a problem. (There may be more than one problematic line.)
z-m-34-02.s.s2.line.0: If the slope of the tangent is m, the tangent is y − 5 = m(x − 3).
z-m-34-02.s.s2.line.1: The distance from the center (0, 0) of the circle to this line must equal the radius 3, so |5 − 3m| / √(m² + 1) = 3.
z-m-34-02.s.s2.line.2: Squaring both sides and simplifying gives 25 − 30m + 9m² = 9m² + 9, so m = 8/15.
z-m-34-02.s.s2.line.3: So the tangent is only y − 5 = (8/15)(x − 3).
z-m-34-02.s.s2.explain: Line 1 assumed that the tangent has a slope, and line 4 is the conclusion 'only one' that came from that assumption. The calculation (lines 2 and 3) is correct. A line with no slope (a line parallel to the y-axis) cannot be written in the form y − 5 = m(x − 3), so it was left out of the solution.
z-m-34-02.s.s3.prompt: Write why only one tangent came out and the equation of the missing tangent, and write one way to check that the line really is a tangent.
z-m-34-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think of a line that Jiho's equation cannot represent for any value of m.
z-m-34-02.s.s3.hint.1: Measure directly the distance from the origin to that line.
z-m-34-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I find and write the equation of the missing line myself?
z-m-34-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I actually check that it is a tangent using the method I wrote?
z-m-34-02.s.s3.model.0: If you put the slope as m, a line standing vertically can't be expressed, so it was left out. The remaining one is x = 3, and the distance from the origin to this line is 3, equal to the radius, so it is a tangent.
z-m-34-02.s.s3.model.1: The line x = 3, parallel to the y-axis, has no slope, so it didn't come out of the equation. Putting x = 3 together with the circle x² + y² = 9, they meet at only the one point (3, 0), so it is a tangent.

z-m-34-03.title: If the coefficients of x squared and y squared are equal, is it always a circle?
z-m-34-03.topic: Equations of figures: the condition for the general form of a circle equation to be a circle
z-m-34-03.goal: Show with a counterexample and by rewriting the expression that x² + y² + (first-degree expression) = 0 can be a circle or not depending on the value of the letter k, and interpret the meaning of the boundary (a single point).
z-m-34-03.material: There is an equation x² + y² + 4x − 2ky + 10 = 0 (k is a real number). Hyeonu said, "The coefficients of x squared and y squared are equal, so whatever k is, this equation represents a circle."
z-m-34-03.thinking.0: Testing whether a generalization always holds
z-m-34-03.thinking.2: Interpreting the meaning of the boundary case
z-m-34-03.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-03.prereq.1: The meaning of the circle equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r²
z-m-34-03.prereq.2: Why r² has to be positive in a circle equation
z-m-34-03.s.s1.prompt: How should Hyeonu's statement be judged?
z-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put values like 0 and 3 in for k one at a time and sort out what shape the equation takes.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.1: Group the terms with x and the terms with y separately and see whether shapes like (x + some number)² and (y − some number)² show up.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.o.a: It is always a circle whatever k is: because the coefficients of x squared and y squared are equal
z-m-34-03.s.s1.r.a: Equal coefficients only mean it might have the form of a circle. Whether the square of the radius is positive must be checked separately.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.o.b: Depending on the value of k, it can be a circle or not
z-m-34-03.s.s1.r.b: You did not just believe 'always' and left open the possibility that it depends on a condition. Let's test this judgment by putting in values of k.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.o.c: Only when k is 0 is it not a circle, and for all other values it is a circle
z-m-34-03.s.s1.r.c: You saw only k = 0 as an exception. Put in a few more values to see whether other k also fail to give a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.o.d: There is no k that gives a circle: the constant term 10 is too large
z-m-34-03.s.s1.r.d: You can test this statement by putting in a large value like k = 3.
z-m-34-03.s.s1.explain: You can't say it's a circle just because the coefficients are equal. You have to rewrite it as squares and check that the right-hand value is positive.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.prompt: Make a counterexample showing that Hyeonu's claim is wrong. Find and enter 3 different integers k for which it is not a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.hint.0: Put k = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... in order, and make a table of how the right-hand value changes when you group the x and y terms.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.hint.1: Separate the cases where the right-hand value is greater than 0 and where it is not.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter it as an integer k.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Rewriting the equation in square form, the right-hand value is 0 or less, so it is not a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.fail.c2: For this k the right-hand value (k squared minus 6) is positive, so it is a circle. Look for values that do not give a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.explain: It rewrites as (x + 2)² + (y − k)² = k² − 6, so it is not a circle when k² ≤ 6. The integers k that fit are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. For k = 3 or −4 it is a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what range of k does not give a circle and how you found that range.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one of the k you entered and rewrite the equation into square form yourself.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find for which k the right-hand value becomes 0.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I explain the condition for the right-hand value to be positive using the expression I wrote?
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I think about what happens at the end (boundary) of the range?
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.model.0: Grouping x and y and rewriting as (x + 2)² + (y − k)² = k² − 6, the square of the radius is k² − 6. If this value is 0 or less it is not a circle, so if the absolute value of k is √6 or less, it is not a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s2.because.model.1: Making it into square form, the right side becomes k squared minus 6. If this value is not greater than 0, there can't be a radius, so every integer from −2 to 2 does not give a circle.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.prompt: When k = √6 (root 6), what figure does the equation x² + y² + 4x − 2ky + 10 = 0 represent?
z-m-34-03.s.s3.hint.0: Find the k for which the right-hand value is 0 and put it into the equation.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.hint.1: Using the fact that a square can't be less than 0, look for which points satisfy the equation.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.o.a: It represents only the single point (−2, √6)
z-m-34-03.s.s3.o.b: It is a circle with center (−2, √6) and radius √6
z-m-34-03.s.s3.r.b: Calculate what the radius is when the right-hand value, k squared minus 6, becomes 0.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.o.c: There is no point at all that satisfies this equation
z-m-34-03.s.s3.r.c: Look for yourself for a point that satisfies (x + 2)² + (y − k)² = 0.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.o.d: It is a very small circle with a radius close to 0
z-m-34-03.s.s3.r.d: It is not 'close to', it is exactly 0. Think about how many points are left when it is exactly 0.
z-m-34-03.s.s3.explain: If k = √6, it is (x + 2)² + (y − √6)² = 0. For a sum of squares to be 0, both squares must be 0, so there is only the one point with x = −2, y = √6.

z-m-34-04.title: If the sum of the squares of the distances to two points is constant, what figure results?
z-m-34-04.topic: Equations of figures: the locus of points whose sum of squared distances to two points is constant
z-m-34-04.goal: Check with an equation a guess made from a few points, and sort out, together with the conditions, how the set of points changes from a circle to a single point to no points at all as the constant changes.
z-m-34-04.material: On a coordinate plane there are two points A(−2, 0), B(2, 0). Think of the collection of all points P(x, y) that satisfy PA² + PB² = k. (PA² is the square of the distance between point P and point A, that is, the distance between P and A squared, and k is a fixed constant.)
z-m-34-04.thinking.0: Forming a hypothesis from little data
z-m-34-04.thinking.1: Checking the hypothesis with an equation
z-m-34-04.thinking.2: Stating the conditions of the conclusion when the constant changes
z-m-34-04.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-04.s.s1.prompt: The data will be revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your idea of what shape the collection of points has.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, separate what has changed from the earlier step and what has stayed the same.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.hint.1: To check whether the figure you chose is right, pick one point and calculate PA² and PB² yourself.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.info: You set k = 16 and tested a few points. P(2, 0), P(0, 2), P(−2, 0) all satisfy PA² + PB² = 16.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What shape do you think all the points that meet the condition make?
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The three points lie on a circle with center at the origin and radius 2. But three points alone cannot confirm 'it is a circle', and it is suitable to hold it as a guess.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All three points are at distance 2 from the origin, so it seems to be a circle. I'd like to check more points too
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a good guess that leaves open how your judgment may change as there are more points.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is a line through the three points
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Compare the coordinates of the three points. You can check whether they lie on one line.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: These three points are all there is. There are no other points
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Calculate whether another point, for example (0, −2), meets the condition.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is certainly a circle, so there is no need to check more
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You can't be sure it is a circle from three points alone. There are many figures that pass through all three points.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Letting the point be P(x, y) and writing in coordinates, PA² = (x + 2)² + y² and PB² = (x − 2)² + y². Adding them and simplifying gives 2x² + 2y² + 8 = k.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: When k = 16, what figure do all the points meeting the condition form?
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If 2x² + 2y² + 8 = 16, then x² + y² = 4. The first guess (a circle) has been confirmed by the equation, and the radius is 2. This is a case where you can keep the guess as it is.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A circle with center at the origin and radius 4
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Calculate what value x² + y² has, and check whether that value is the square of the radius or the radius.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A circle with center at the origin and radius 2
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The guess was confirmed by the equation. This conclusion came from calculating that the square of the radius is 4.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The points at the same distance from A and B, that is, the y-axis
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The condition is not PA = PB, but that PA² + PB² is constant.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: A circle with center at the origin and radius 8
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: When dividing 2x² + 2y² + 8 = 16 by 2, check whether you handled the 8 as well.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Simplifying gives x² + y² = (k − 8)/2. Now change k and look at the cases k = 8 and k = 4.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: When k = 8 and when k = 4, what happens to the points meeting the condition?
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If k = 8, then x² + y² = 0, so there is only the origin, and if k = 4, then x² + y² = −2, so no point satisfies it. It is a circle only when k > 8. The first guess changed into a conclusion with the condition that k is in a certain range.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: As k gets smaller, the circle gets smaller too: if k = 8 the radius is 2, and if k = 4 the radius is 1
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Calculate what you get when you put k = 8 into (k − 8)/2.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: A circle is made whatever k is, and at k = 4 it is a circle with a negative radius
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A radius is a distance, so it can't be negative. Think about whether there is a point satisfying x² + y² = (negative number).
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If k = 8 it is just the one point, the origin, and if k = 4 there is no such point at all
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You decided the number of points by considering when x² + y² is 0 or negative.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: If k = 8 there is no such point, and if k = 4 it is the one point, the origin
z-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Check whether the value you get by putting k = 8 and k = 4 into (k − 8)/2 is 0 or negative.
z-m-34-04.s.s1.reflect: What happened to the guess you made from the first three points after you checked it with the equation? And when k changes, which part of the conclusion was revised by adding a condition?
z-m-34-04.s.s2.prompt: Write out how the collection of points P changes depending on the value of k. (Include at which values of k it changes.)
z-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.0: Separate the cases where the right-hand value of x² + y² = (k − 8)/2 is positive, 0, and negative.
z-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.1: Put in k = 8, k = 20, and k = 0 and check the collection of points yourself.
z-m-34-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I write down, without leaving any out, what shape it is on each side of the boundary value?
z-m-34-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I treat the case k = 8 separately?
z-m-34-04.s.s2.model.0: If k is greater than 8, it is a circle with its center at the origin, if k = 8 it is just the one point, the origin, and if k is less than 8 there is no point that meets the condition.

z-m-34-05.title: If the slope is between the slopes to the two endpoints, does the line meet the segment?
z-m-34-05.topic: Equations of figures: the condition for a line through a point to meet a segment (the range of the slope)
z-m-34-05.goal: Test the claim 'between the slopes to the two endpoints' with specific slopes to build a counterexample, and state the range of slopes that do meet and the whole answer including the line with no slope.
z-m-34-05.material: On a coordinate plane there are a point P(2, 0) and a segment AB. A(0, 3), B(5, 3), and segment AB, including both endpoints, is the part of y = 3 where x is from 0 to 5. You want to find the range of m for which a line l through P with slope m meets segment AB. Seorin said, "The slope of the line from P to A is −3/2 and the slope of the line to B is 1. So if −3/2 ≤ m ≤ 1, it meets the segment."
z-m-34-05.thinking.0: Testing a generalization with specific values
z-m-34-05.thinking.1: Finding both sides of the range without missing any
z-m-34-05.thinking.2: Checking exceptions such as a line with no slope
z-m-34-05.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-05.prereq.1: The equation of a line through a point with slope m
z-m-34-05.prereq.2: The meaning of a line meeting a segment (endpoints included)
z-m-34-05.s.s1.prompt: You want to test whether Seorin's claim is right. What is the most trustworthy test?
z-m-34-05.s.s1.hint.0: Draw P(2, 0) and segment AB on a coordinate plane and draw the lines from P to A and to B.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one slope inside the range the claim talks about and draw that line.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.o.a: Check only the lines through the two endpoints A and B, for m = −3/2 and m = 1
z-m-34-05.s.s1.r.a: The two lines through the endpoints obviously meet. This does not test the values inside the range the claim talks about.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.o.b: Sketch a rough picture, and if it feels like it lies somewhere between the two endpoints, move on
z-m-34-05.s.s1.r.b: A feeling alone can't tell you whether a value inside the interval really meets. You have to put in a specific value and check.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.o.c: Pick one value inside the interval the claim allows and check whether that line meets the segment
z-m-34-05.s.s1.r.c: The claim says 'everything inside works', so if even one value inside fails, the claim collapses. Testing with a value inside the interval is the most direct.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.o.d: Write it down as 'the range of slopes is always between the slopes to the two endpoints' and move on
z-m-34-05.s.s1.r.d: You memorized it like a general rule. You did not check whether it is right for this position of the point P and the segment.
z-m-34-05.s.s1.explain: The claim says 'for every m inside the interval, it meets'. If you pick one value inside and it does not meet, the claim is wrong. For example, you can test m = 0.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.prompt: Enter 4 different values of m for which the line with slope m meets segment AB. Test values both inside and outside Seorin's range.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.0: Express in terms of m the x-coordinate where the line y = m(x − 2) is at y = 3, and check whether that x is from 0 to 5.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.1: Separate the cases where m is positive and negative, put in values one at a time, and make a table of whether it meets.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The line y = m(x − 2) meets segment AB (endpoints included).
z-m-34-05.s.s2.fail.c1: A line with this slope does not meet segment AB. Check the x-coordinate at y = 3 to see whether the line and the segment really meet anywhere.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.explain: It meets if m ≤ −3/2 or m ≥ 1. Between −3/2 and 1 (for example 0, 0.5, −1), it does not meet. The range Seorin gave is not the 'range where they meet' but the 'range where they do not meet'.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain, using one specific value of m, why Seorin's range (−3/2 ≤ m ≤ 1) is wrong.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one slope inside the range, put y = 3 into y = m(x − 2), and find x.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare whether the x you found is inside the x range of the segment (0 to 5).
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I actually put the value I used into the equation of the line to check?
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I go beyond saying the range is 'wrong' and say which side is right?
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.model.0: If m = 0, the line is the x-axis itself, so it does not meet the segment on y = 3. It is a value inside the interval and it still does not meet, so the first idea is wrong.
z-m-34-05.s.s2.because.model.1: When m = −1, y = −(x − 2) has x = −1 at y = 3, which is outside the segment. Even if the slope is between the two end slopes, it meets outside the segment.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.prompt: Consider all lines through P (including the line with no slope, x = 2). How can you describe the lines that meet segment AB?
z-m-34-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find yourself the coordinates where the line x = 2 passes through segment AB.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.hint.1: Combine it with the range of m you checked in the earlier step and put it together in one sentence.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.o.a: −3/2 ≤ m ≤ 1, and the line with no slope, x = 2, does not meet
z-m-34-05.s.s3.r.a: You already checked earlier that values in this range do not meet. The range is on the opposite side.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.o.b: m ≤ −3/2 or m ≥ 1, and the line with no slope, x = 2, also meets
z-m-34-05.s.s3.o.c: m ≤ −3/2 or m ≥ 1, and the line with no slope, x = 2, does not meet
z-m-34-05.s.s3.r.c: The range of the slope is right. Check yourself whether the line x = 2 meets segment AB.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.o.d: It meets for every m, and the line with no slope meets too
z-m-34-05.s.s3.r.d: Check whether the line with m = 0 meets the segment.
z-m-34-05.s.s3.explain: x = 2 and y = 3 meet at the point (2, 3), and this point is on segment AB (0 ≤ 2 ≤ 5). So the lines with m ≤ −3/2 or m ≥ 1 and the vertical line x = 2 all meet the segment. If you look only at lines that have a slope, it is easy to miss this line.

z-m-34-06.title: On the x-axis, is there only one point at equal distance from two lines?
z-m-34-06.topic: Equations of figures: finding a point from conditions on its distance to lines
z-m-34-06.goal: Find and check that there can be two points on the x-axis at equal distance from two lines, and judge, together with the condition, how the number changes if the two lines are parallel.
z-m-34-06.material: There are a line l₁: 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 and a line l₂: 4x + 3y − 9 = 0. You want to find a point P(t, 0) on the x-axis whose distances to the two lines are equal. Minseo found P(3, 0), checked that both distances are 3/5, and said, "This is the only point with equal distances."
z-m-34-06.thinking.0: Doubting whether the solution you found is all of them
z-m-34-06.thinking.2: Judging that the number of answers changes depending on a condition (whether the lines are parallel)
z-m-34-06.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-06.prereq.1: The meaning of the distance between a point and a line
z-m-34-06.prereq.2: The meaning of expressions with absolute values
z-m-34-06.s.s1.prompt: Is there only one, as Minseo says? Predict how many points on the x-axis have equal distances to the two lines.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the two distances for t = 3 and check that they are equal, then compare what happens when you put in t = 0 and t = 4.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.hint.1: In the formula for the distance from a point to a line, look at what the denominator is and what signs the value inside the absolute value can have.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.o.a: 0: the distances to the two lines are always different on the x-axis
z-m-34-06.s.s1.r.a: Minseo already found one point, P(3, 0), where the distances are equal. It is not 0.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.o.b: 1: if you set the distances equal and solve, one value of t comes out
z-m-34-06.s.s1.r.b: Check with other values of t whether the point Minseo found is really all of them. The distance formula has an absolute value.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.o.c: Infinitely many: points with equal distances are everywhere on the x-axis
z-m-34-06.s.s1.r.c: Calculate the two distances yourself for t = 0 and check whether they are equal.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.o.d: 2: it seems one point with equal distances will come out on each side
z-m-34-06.s.s1.r.d: You did not stop after finding one point and doubted whether there are more. You have to actually solve the equation to check.
z-m-34-06.s.s1.explain: You have checked that P(3, 0) is one, but you only find out whether there are more by solving the equation. Let's find them yourself in the next step.
z-m-34-06.s.s2.prompt: Among the points P(t, 0) on the x-axis, find 2 different points whose distances to the two lines l₁ and l₂ are equal, and enter t.
z-m-34-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the two distance formulas and see whether the denominators are the same. If they are, think about what relationship the numerators must have.
z-m-34-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think, with number examples (for example 3 and −3), about what relationship two numbers with the same absolute value can have.
z-m-34-06.s.s2.var.t: The x-coordinate t of the point P
z-m-34-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The distances from P(t, 0) to the two lines are equal. (The denominators for both lines are 5, the same.)
z-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The two distances are not equal. Find the distance to each line and compare.
z-m-34-06.s.s2.explain: There are two points, t = 3 and t = −3. When t = −3, both distances are 21/5. This is because when you remove the absolute value, two cases come out, the same sign and the opposite sign. The two points are where the two lines that bisect the angle between the two lines (y = x + 3 and x + y = 3) meet the x-axis.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.prompt: This time the two lines have changed to be parallel. When l₁: 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 and l₃: 3x + 4y + 8 = 0, how many points on the x-axis are at equal distance from the two lines?
z-m-34-06.s.s3.hint.0: Put in t = 2/3 and t = 0 and calculate the two distances for each.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.hint.1: Use the method from before on these two lines as it is and check whether both cases are possible.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.o.a: 1: the line exactly in the middle of the two parallel lines meets the x-axis at one point
z-m-34-06.s.s3.o.b: 2: as in the earlier problem, two places come out on the x-axis
z-m-34-06.s.s3.r.b: Earlier the two lines met each other. Check with an equation whether two places also come out in the same way when they are parallel.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.o.c: 0: two parallel lines do not meet, so there is no point at equal distance
z-m-34-06.s.s3.r.c: Not meeting is different from there being no point at equal distance. Think about the middle between the two parallel lines.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.o.d: Infinitely many: if the lines are parallel, every point has equal distances
z-m-34-06.s.s3.r.d: Calculate the two distances for t = 0 and check whether they are really equal.
z-m-34-06.s.s3.explain: In |3t − 12| = |3t + 8|, 3t − 12 = 3t + 8 does not hold, and 3t − 12 = −(3t + 8) gives only t = 2/3. When the lines are parallel, one of the cases from removing the absolute value disappears, so the number decreases. The first guess (2) changes depending on the condition.

z-m-34-07.title: If the origin makes it false, is the opposite side the region?
z-m-34-07.topic: Equations of figures: regions divided by a line and inequalities (choosing a test point)
z-m-34-07.goal: Discover that a test point lying on the boundary line cannot tell which side is the region, and decide the region with a suitable test point.
z-m-34-07.material: You want to show the region represented by the inequality y > 2x on a coordinate plane. Sangu's solution is below. (Line numbers are shown starting from 1.)
z-m-34-07.thinking.0: Finding the hidden assumption of the solution
z-m-34-07.thinking.1: Judging the conditions for a test point
z-m-34-07.thinking.2: Fixing it and deciding the region
z-m-34-07.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-07.prereq.1: How to draw the line y = 2x on a coordinate plane
z-m-34-07.prereq.2: The meaning of a point that satisfies an inequality
z-m-34-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Sangu's solution. (There may be more than one wrong line.)
z-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute the numbers each line talks about and check whether they are right.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check where the origin is relative to the line y = 2x.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.line.0: The boundary is the line y = 2x, and the inequality sign has no equal sign, so draw the boundary as a dotted line.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.line.1: Putting the origin (0, 0) in as the test point gives 0 > 0, which is false.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.line.2: The origin does not satisfy the inequality, so the side opposite the one where the origin is is the region.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.line.3: So the region of y > 2x is below the line.
z-m-34-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The origin is on the boundary y = 2x, so there is no such thing as 'the side where the origin is'. The conclusion in line 4 (below) is also wrong because of that. Lines 1 and 2 are right.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.prompt: To decide which side of the line the region is on, pick one test point and put it into y > 2x. Choose all the points that can be used as a test point.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, put its x-coordinate into y = 2x and compare with its y-coordinate.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.1: Pick two points that are not on the boundary and check whether their results point to the same side.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.r.a: The origin is on the boundary, so it belongs to neither side.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.r.b: This point also satisfies y = 2x, so it is on the boundary. It can't tell you which side is the region.
z-m-34-07.s.s2.explain: Any point that is not on the boundary y = 2x can be a test point. For (1, 0), 0 > 2 is false, so the opposite side (above) is the region, and for (−1, 1), 1 > −2 is true, so this side (above) is the region. The results of the two points point to the same region.
z-m-34-07.s.s3.prompt: Write where Sangu's solution went wrong, and choose a test point to use instead of the origin to decide which side of the line the region is on.
z-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write whether the test point makes y > 2x true or false.
z-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.1: Use the fact that if it is true, the side with the test point is the region, and if it is false, the opposite side is the region.
z-m-34-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I check that the test point I chose is not on the boundary?
z-m-34-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I decide the side of the region to match the result (true/false) of the test point?
z-m-34-07.s.s3.model.0: The origin is a point on the line y = 2x, so it can't tell which side it belongs to. Putting in (0, 1) gives 1 > 0, which is true, so the region is above the line.
z-m-34-07.s.s3.model.1: (0, 0) is on the boundary, so it can't be a test point. For (1, 0), 0 > 2 is false, so the region is the opposite side, the upper side.

z-m-34-08.title: Does the line obtained from the equations of two circles always pass through the intersection points?
z-m-34-08.topic: Equations of figures: the line obtained from the equations of two circles (the position of two circles)
z-m-34-08.goal: Test with examples under what conditions the rule that the line obtained by subtracting the equations of two circles passes through their intersection points can be used, and state the conditions for applying the rule yourself.
z-m-34-08.material: There is a circle C₁: x² + y² = 4 (center (0, 0), radius 2). Seoa learned the rule "The line obtained by subtracting the equations of two circles side by side is a line through the common points of the two circles." You will look at whether this rule can be used in every case, changing the new circle one at a time.
z-m-34-08.thinking.0: Examining the conditions under which the rule holds
z-m-34-08.thinking.1: Revising your judgment with new data
z-m-34-08.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-08.prereq.1: The equation of a circle and the position of two circles (the relationship between the distance between centers and the radii)
z-m-34-08.prereq.2: The meaning of a point that satisfies two equations together
z-m-34-08.s.s1.prompt: The data will be revealed one at a time. Choose your judgment each time.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, compare the distance between the centers of the two circles with the sum of the radii.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.hint.1: Pick a point on the line and put it directly into the equations of the two circles.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.info: You brought in the circle C₂: (x − 2)² + y² = 4 (center (2, 0), radius 2). Subtracting the equations of C₁ and C₂ side by side and simplifying gave the line x = 1.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: Does the line x = 1 pass through the points where the two circles meet?
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.after: (1, √3) and (1, −√3) are points that satisfy the equations of both circles, and both are on x = 1. In this case the rule fits well.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: There is no relationship: subtracting equations is just a calculation and has nothing to do with the properties of figures
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: An intersection point is a point that satisfies both equations. The subtracted equation is also 0 at that point. The calculation has a meaning in terms of the figures.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It passes through them: an intersection point of the two circles satisfies both equations, so it satisfies the subtracted equation too
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You gave the reason that if there are intersection points, they lie on the subtracted equation. Let's test with the next data in which direction this reason is true.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The two circles do not meet: because if a line equation comes out, it is not a circle
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The result of subtracting circle equations being a line and whether the two circles meet are separate matters. Put (1, √3) into each equation.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It passes through them: putting (1, √3) into the equations of the two circles, both hold, and this point is on x = 1
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You checked by direct substitution. You checked one point, so you have not checked the whole rule, but it is enough evidence for this case.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.info: This time you brought in the circle C₃: (x − 6)² + y² = 4 (center (6, 0), radius 2). Subtracting the equations of C₁ and C₃ side by side and simplifying gave the line x = 3.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Does the line x = 3 pass through common points of the two circles?
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.after: C₁ exists only where x is from −2 to 2, so there is no point of C₁ on x = 3. The rule is only 'if there are intersection points, they are on the subtracted equation', and it does not say that there are intersection points just because the subtracted equation is a line. The earlier judgment has to be corrected by attaching a condition.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: There is a common point on x = 3: the method is the same as before, so the result is the same
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even if the method is the same, the position of the circle has changed. Check what range the x-coordinates of C₁ are in.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: There is no common point on x = 3: C₁ exists only where x is 2 or less
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You checked the range directly from the center and radius of the circle. Even when a line comes out of the equations, you have to check separately whether there are common points.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: x = 3 is close to the center of C₃, so it meets only C₃
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The x-coordinates of C₃ range from 4 to 8. Check whether the line x = 3 meets C₃.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Even if a line came out, whether there is a common point has to be checked separately, so don't decide yet
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a careful judgment. But if you look at the range of the circles, you can decide right away.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Finally you brought in the circle C₄: (x − 4)² + y² = 4 (center (4, 0), radius 2). Subtracting the equations of C₁ and C₄ side by side and simplifying gave the line x = 2.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the relationship between the line x = 2 and the two circles C₁, C₄?
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.after: (2, 0) is the only common point that satisfies the equations of both C₁ and C₄, and it is on x = 2. In this case x = 2 is the line that is tangent to both circles. The rule holds even when there is one intersection point.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: There are two intersection points of the two circles on x = 2
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Put x = 2 into the equation of C₁ and calculate what y is.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The two circles meet at the one point (2, 0), and the line x = 2 passes through that point
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even when there is one intersection point (the touching case), the subtracted equation passes through that point. You can check by direct substitution.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The two circles do not meet, so x = 2 has no meaning
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Check whether (2, 0) satisfies the equations of both circles.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: x = 2 meets only C₁ and does not meet C₄
z-m-34-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Put (2, 0) into the equation of C₄.
z-m-34-08.s.s1.reflect: Was the first rule right in some cases, and did conditions get attached in others? How is 'if there are intersection points, they are on the line' different from 'if a line comes out, there are intersection points'?
z-m-34-08.s.s2.prompt: You got a line by subtracting the equations of two circles side by side. Before saying that the line passes through the common points of the two circles, write what you must check first, and give one example where the result is different.

z-m-34-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the distance between the centers when the two circles meet and when they do not.
z-m-34-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I make clear that what must be checked is 'whether there are intersection points'?
z-m-34-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: In the example I gave, can you see that a line comes out but there are no intersection points (or just one)?
z-m-34-08.s.s2.model.0: You have to compare the distance between the centers of the two circles with the radii and first check whether the two circles actually meet. If they are far apart, like circles with radius 2 and centers at 0 and 6, then even if the subtracted equation gives the line x = 3, there is no common point.
z-m-34-08.s.s2.model.1: You have to check that the distance between the centers is not greater than the sum of the radii. If two circles of radius 2 have centers 6 apart, they do not meet, yet a line like x = 3 still comes out.

z-m-34-09.title: If you change the vertex of a right triangle, does the circumcenter stay the same?
z-m-34-09.topic: Equations of figures: a right triangle and its circumcenter (finding a point from distance conditions)
z-m-34-09.goal: Test with lattice-point examples the guess that the circumcenter does not change when one side is fixed and the right-angle vertex moves, and tell apart what changes when the angle is not a right angle.
z-m-34-09.material: On a coordinate plane there are A(0, 0), B(10, 0). The point C(p, q) is placed with q > 0, with integer coordinates (a lattice point), and so that ∠C = 90°. The circumcenter of triangle ABC is the point at equal distance from the three vertices A, B, C. Ian said, "If I change the position of C, the circumcenter will move along with it."
z-m-34-09.thinking.0: Testing a guess with several examples
z-m-34-09.thinking.1: Finding a property common to the examples
z-m-34-09.thinking.2: Judging how the conclusion changes when the condition changes
z-m-34-09.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-09.prereq.1: The meaning of the circumcenter (the point at equal distance from the three vertices of a triangle)
z-m-34-09.prereq.3: The relationship between directions when two lines are perpendicular
z-m-34-09.s.s1.prompt: What happens to the circumcenter when you change C while keeping ∠C = 90°? Choose based on what you think now.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.hint.0: Fix one C with ∠C = 90° and roughly sketch where the circumcenter is.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.hint.1: Fix one more C and compare whether the circumcenter is in the same place.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.o.a: The circumcenter does not change wherever C is: it is always the same point
z-m-34-09.s.s1.o.b: The circumcenter changes with the position of C: because the vertex changes
z-m-34-09.s.s1.r.b: Like Ian, you thought that if the vertex changes, the circumcenter will change. Check in real examples whether the circumcenter moves.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.o.c: The circumcenter is always the same point as the right-angle vertex C
z-m-34-09.s.s1.r.c: If the distance from the circumcenter to C is 0, the distances to A and B would have to be 0 too. Think about whether that can be.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.o.d: In a right triangle, the circumcenter always lies outside the triangle
z-m-34-09.s.s1.r.d: You judged only by the shape, without finding the position of the circumcenter. Find the position in one example.
z-m-34-09.s.s1.explain: This judgment will be tested in the next step by making lattice points C yourself. Either way, it is important to check with examples.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different lattice points C(p, q) that satisfy ∠C = 90°. (q > 0, p and q are integers)
z-m-34-09.s.s2.hint.0: For C to be a right angle, think about what relationship the direction from C to A and the direction from C to B must have.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.hint.1: Change p from 1 to 9 and make a table to check whether q is an integer.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.hint.2: Measure and compare the distances from the points you found to (5, 0).
z-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c2: p and q must be integers.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The two directions from C to A and to B are perpendicular, so ∠C is a right angle.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.fail.c3: ∠C is not a right angle. Add the product of the horizontal parts and the product of the vertical parts of the change from C to A and the change from C to B, and check whether it is 0.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.explain: The lattice points C that satisfy the condition are (1, 3), (2, 4), (5, 5), (8, 4), (9, 3). All of these points are at distance 5 from (5, 0). That is, they are points on the circle with AB as a diameter.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Write where the circumcenter is for the C's you found and why it ends up in the same place.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: For one of the C's you found, look for a point that is at equal distance from A, B, and that C.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about the shape formed by the points you found (whether they are on one circle).
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Can the coordinates of the circumcenter I wrote be checked in at least one of the C's I found?
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I explain 'why it is the same place' with distances or a circle?
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The points (1, 3), (5, 5), (9, 3) that I found are all at distance 5 from (5, 0), so the point at equal distance from the three vertices A, B, C is (5, 0). That is, the midpoint of AB is the circumcenter.
z-m-34-09.s.s2.because.model.1: When C is a right angle, C is on the circle with AB as its diameter, so the distances from the center (5, 0) to A, B, C are all equal to the radius 5. So the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse AB.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.prompt: This time it is triangle ABC with the vertex C(5, 6), where ∠C is not a right angle. Where is the circumcenter?
z-m-34-09.s.s3.hint.0: Find the line on which the points at equal distance from A and B lie.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.hint.1: For a point (5, y) on that line, find y so that its distance to A and its distance to C are equal.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.o.a: It is still (5, 0): the circumcenter is fixed as the midpoint of side AB
z-m-34-09.s.s3.r.a: Compare the distance from (5, 0) to C(5, 6) with the distance to A.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.o.b: It is not on the line x = 5: because C has changed
z-m-34-09.s.s3.r.b: The circumcenter is a point at equal distance from A and B. Think about what line such points lie on.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.o.c: It is on the line x = 5, but it is not (5, 0)
z-m-34-09.s.s3.o.d: There is no circumcenter: if it is not a right angle, there is no circle through the three vertices
z-m-34-09.s.s3.r.d: A triangle that is not a right triangle also has a circumscribed circle. A right angle only changes where the circumcenter is.
z-m-34-09.s.s3.explain: The points at equal distance from A and B lie on the line x = 5. Among them, the point at equal distance from C(5, 6) too is (5, 11/12). From (5, 0), the distance to C is 6 and to A is 5, so it is not the circumcenter. The circumcenter being constant was because of the condition ∠C = 90°.

z-m-34-10.title: What do you need to know about the point C to fix the area of the triangle?
z-m-34-10.topic: Equations of figures: the area of a triangle and conditions on the position of a point (sufficiency of information)
z-m-34-10.goal: Sort out what information about a point is needed and what is not enough for the area of a triangle to be fixed, and explain the set of points that make the same area.
z-m-34-10.material: On a coordinate plane there are two points A(0, 0), B(6, 0). The coordinates of the point C are not known yet. You want to find the area of triangle ABC, and you will examine whether a single piece of information about the point C is enough to fix the area. (Assume the point C is not on the line through segment AB, so a triangle is formed.)
z-m-34-10.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-34-10.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the same condition
z-m-34-10.thinking.2: Describing the set of points that satisfy the condition
z-m-34-10.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-10.prereq.1: The base and height of a triangle on a coordinate plane
z-m-34-10.prereq.2: The distance between a point and the x-axis
z-m-34-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information below for which that information alone fixes the area of triangle ABC.
z-m-34-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, plot two points that C could be, and compare whether the heights of the triangle are the same.
z-m-34-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how to read the height when the base AB is on the x-axis.
z-m-34-10.s.s1.o.a: The point C is on the line y = x
z-m-34-10.s.s1.r.a: The height changes depending on where on y = x the point C is. Compare the areas at (1, 1) and (5, 5).
z-m-34-10.s.s1.o.b: The point C is on the line y = 4
z-m-34-10.s.s1.o.c: The x-coordinate of the point C is 2
z-m-34-10.s.s1.r.c: The x-coordinate alone does not tell you the height from the base, so the area is not fixed. Compare (2, 1) and (2, 5).
z-m-34-10.s.s1.o.d: The point C is on the circle x² + y² = 25
z-m-34-10.s.s1.r.d: Points on a circle have many different heights. Compare the heights near (5, 0) and at (0, 5).
z-m-34-10.s.s1.o.e: The y-coordinate of the point C is −3
z-m-34-10.s.s1.explain: The area is fixed by the base AB (length 6) and the height, and the height is the absolute value of the y-coordinate of C. Only the information that tells you the y-coordinate (its absolute value) is enough. If y = 4, the height is 4, so the area is 12, and if the y-coordinate is −3, the height is 3, so the area is 9. For the others, several heights are possible.
z-m-34-10.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different points C(x, y) for which the area of triangle ABC is 12. (The coordinates are integers.)
z-m-34-10.s.s2.hint.0: First find what the height must be on the base 6 for the area to be 12.
z-m-34-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check with one example whether the x-coordinate can be different as long as the height is right.
z-m-34-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter x and y as integers.
z-m-34-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The area of triangle ABC is 12. (Base 6, height is the absolute value of y.)
z-m-34-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The area of triangle ABC is not 12. Find the area from the length of the base AB and the height of C.
z-m-34-10.s.s2.explain: The height just needs to be 4, so y = 4 or y = −4, and x can be any integer. For example, (1, 4), (7, 4), (3, −4) all meet the condition.
z-m-34-10.s.s3.prompt: If you collect all the points C for which the area of triangle ABC is 12, what figure do they make?
z-m-34-10.s.s3.hint.0: Collect the y-coordinates of the points you found earlier. What values come out?
z-m-34-10.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether there are points only above the x-axis or below it as well.
z-m-34-10.s.s3.o.a: All the points on the circle with AB as a diameter
z-m-34-10.s.s3.r.a: Points on a circle have many different heights. Compare (3, 3) and (5, 0).
z-m-34-10.s.s3.o.b: Just the one line y = 4 (points only above the x-axis)
z-m-34-10.s.s3.r.b: There is not only one side where the height is 4. Think about points below the x-axis too.
z-m-34-10.s.s3.r.c: In the earlier step, points with different x-coordinates all met the condition.
z-m-34-10.s.s3.o.d: The line y = 4 and the line y = −4, two lines
z-m-34-10.s.s3.explain: For the area to be 12, the absolute value of the y-coordinate of C must be 4. One line above and one below the x-axis both meet the condition. This connects to the original 'sufficiency of information' in that even the same information doesn't give just one answer.

z-m-34-11.title: If you turn the slope upside down, is it the reflected line?
z-m-34-11.topic: Equations of figures: reflection in the line y = x (comparing two methods)
z-m-34-11.goal: Compare two methods for finding the reflection in the line y = x, decide which is trustworthy, and find and explain a case where the reciprocal-of-the-slope rule does not hold (a horizontal line).
z-m-34-11.material: Let l' be the line obtained by reflecting the line l: y = 2x + 1 in the line y = x. Gaon said, "A point (x, y) on l is moved to (y, x), so just swap x and y in the equation," and got y = (x − 1)/2. Jian said, "The slope becomes its reciprocal and the y-intercept stays the same," and got y = x/2 + 1. The slopes of the two results are the same but the equations are different.
z-m-34-11.thinking.0: Choosing a way to decide when two methods give different results
z-m-34-11.thinking.1: Finding the limits of where a rule applies
z-m-34-11.thinking.2: Comparing and evaluating methods in writing
z-m-34-11.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-11.prereq.1: Reflection of a point (the coordinates of the point (a, b) reflected in the line y = x)
z-m-34-11.prereq.2: The equation of a line, slope, and intercepts
z-m-34-11.s.s1.prompt: What is a trustworthy way to decide which of the two results is right?
z-m-34-11.s.s1.hint.0: Find one point on l and write (x, y) and (y, x) for it.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.hint.1: Substitute the point into the two equations and compare whether they hold.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.o.a: The simpler equation is more likely to be right, so trust Gaon's result
z-m-34-11.s.s1.r.a: An equation being simple has nothing to do with whether it is right. You have to test by putting in numbers.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.o.b: The slopes of both results are 1/2, so both are considered right
z-m-34-11.s.s1.r.b: Even if the slopes are the same, lines with different intercepts are different lines. Check whether a single line l' is determined.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.o.c: Put the point obtained by swapping x and y of a point on l into the two equations
z-m-34-11.s.s1.r.c: The reflected point must be on l'. One point can tell the two results apart.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.o.d: Substitute the point where l and y = x meet into the lines of both results to see whether it is on them
z-m-34-11.s.s1.r.d: A point on y = x does not move under the reflection. The intersection is a point that must also be on l'. This method is right too.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.explain: The point (0, 1) on l is moved to (1, 0). Substituting into Gaon's equation it holds, and in Jian's equation it gives 1.5, so it does not hold. The intersection (−1, −1) does not move, so it must be on l' as well, and again Gaon's is right and Jian's is wrong.
z-m-34-11.s.s1.acc.0: The intersection of l and y = x does not move under the reflection, so it must also be on l'. Checking in which equation this point holds is also a trustworthy method.
z-m-34-11.s.s2.prompt: What is the line obtained by reflecting the line l: y = 3 (a horizontal line) in the line y = x?
z-m-34-11.s.s2.hint.0: Pick three points on l and write the points you get by changing (x, y) to (y, x).
z-m-34-11.s.s2.hint.1: Check what line the swapped points lie along.
z-m-34-11.s.s2.r.b: Check whether the points obtained by swapping x and y of the points (0, 3) and (1, 3) on l lie on y = 3.
z-m-34-11.s.s2.r.c: Check whether the point (3, 0) obtained by swapping the point (0, 3) lies on y = 1/3.
z-m-34-11.s.s2.o.d: There is no reflected line: because the reciprocal of the slope 0 can't be found
z-m-34-11.s.s2.r.d: Not being able to find the reciprocal of the slope means that rule can't be used, not that the reflected line does not exist. Swap the points and check.
z-m-34-11.s.s2.explain: A point (t, 3) on the horizontal line is moved to (3, t). These points are all on the line x = 3. The reciprocal-of-the-slope rule can't be used on a horizontal line with slope 0, but the method of swapping points can be used.
z-m-34-11.s.s3.prompt: Compare the two methods and write which is more trustworthy and when the rule 'take the reciprocal of the slope' can't be used.
z-m-34-11.s.s3.hint.0: Test whether each method can be used on any line, with lines like y = 3 and y = −x + 4.
z-m-34-11.s.s3.hint.1: For each method, write in one sentence 'when it can't be used'.
z-m-34-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is my judgment based on the results of the tests (substitution)?
z-m-34-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I give one example where the reciprocal rule doesn't work?
z-m-34-11.s.s3.model.0: The method of swapping x and y of a point can be used on any line, so it is more trustworthy. The reciprocal-of-the-slope rule can't find a reciprocal for a horizontal line with slope 0, so it can't be used there, and the intercept also has to be calculated separately.
z-m-34-11.s.s3.model.1: If you pick a point on l and substitute it with x and y swapped, you can tell which equation is right. The method of taking the reciprocal of the slope can't be used on a horizontal line like y = 3.

z-m-34-12.title: Is the minimum distance between a circle and a line always the distance minus the radius?
z-m-34-12.topic: Equations of figures: minimum and maximum distance between a point on a circle and a line
z-m-34-12.goal: Judge how the rule 'subtract the radius from the distance from the center to the line' changes depending on the positions of the line and the circle, and sort out the rules for the minimum and maximum together with their conditions.
z-m-34-12.material: There is a circle C: (x − 1)² + (y − 1)² = 4 (center (1, 1), radius 2) and a line l_k: x + y = k. You want to find out how the distance from a point P to the line l_k changes as P moves on the circle. Haeun knows the rule "The minimum is (distance from the center to the line) − (radius)." The distance from the center (1, 1) to the line x + y = k is |2 − k| / √2.
z-m-34-12.thinking.0: Testing the range where a rule applies
z-m-34-12.thinking.1: Revising your judgment depending on the position
z-m-34-12.prereq.0: Assumption: the 'H3' of this task is only a difficulty label from the production stage, not a grade placement in the curriculum. It assumes students who have learned middle school math and the first part of high school Common Mathematics 'equations of figures' (the coordinate plane, equations of lines and circles).
z-m-34-12.prereq.1: Reading the center and radius from the equation of a circle
z-m-34-12.prereq.2: The meaning of the distance between a point and a line
z-m-34-12.prereq.3: The position of a circle and a line
z-m-34-12.s.s1.prompt: Look at it while changing the value of k. Choose your judgment each time.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.hint.0: For each k, compare the distance from the center to the line with the radius 2.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a picture of the point on the circle closest to the line and the point farthest from it.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.info: When k = 8, the distance from the center to the line is 6/√2 = 3√2 (about 4.24).
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.ask: When the point P moves on the circle, what is the minimum distance from P to the line?
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.after: The line x + y = 8 is outside the circle, so the distance to the point on the circle closest to the line is 3√2 − 2. The rule fits well.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This value is the distance to the point farthest from the line. The minimum is the nearer point.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This value is the distance to the center. A point on the circle can get closer to the line than the center is.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Using Haeun's rule as it is fits this case. The line is outside the circle, so the nearer point is closer by the radius.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.0.r.d: 2 is the radius of the circle. It can't be used directly as the distance to the line.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.info: This time k = 4. The distance from the center to the line is 2/√2 = √2 (about 1.41), less than the radius 2. Using the rule as it is gives √2 − 2 ≈ −0.59.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.ask: When the point P moves on the circle, what is the minimum distance?
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.after: If the distance from the center to the line is less than the radius, the line passes through the circle. Then there are points on the circle that are on the line, so the minimum is 0. The earlier rule needs a condition attached so that it can be used only when the line is outside the circle.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.o.a: −0.59 (the value calculated from the rule as it is)
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A distance can't be negative. A negative calculated result is a sign that the rule doesn't fit this case.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 0: the line meets the circle, so there are points on the circle that are on the line
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If the line passes through the circle, some points on the circle are on the line. The distance at that point is 0.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 0.59 (the absolute value of the rule's calculated value)
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Check what the absolute value is the distance to. Look at whether the line and the circle meet.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This value is the distance from the center to the line. Points on the circle can get closer.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.info: With the same k = 4, this time look at the maximum distance to the line when the point P moves on the circle.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.after: The maximum is the distance to the center plus the radius, so it is the same rule even if the line passes through the circle. The difference is that the rule for the minimum changes with the position, while the maximum does not change.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even if the line passes through the circle, the point on the circle farthest from the line is on the side opposite the center. It is the distance to the center plus the radius.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the radius minus the distance to the center. It has nothing to do with the distance to the farthest point.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The radius does not become the maximum. Work out the distance to the point farthest from the line.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The line passes through the circle, so the maximum can't be determined
z-m-34-12.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even if the line passes through the circle, the maximum of the distances from the line to the points on the circle is determined.
z-m-34-12.s.s1.reflect: When k was 8 the rule was right, but how did it have to be fixed at k = 4? Which point differed in the rules for the minimum and the maximum?
z-m-34-12.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite Haeun's rule for the minimum distance between the circle and the line l_k, attaching the needed condition.
z-m-34-12.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the distance to the center with the radius at k = 8, 4, and 2 + 2√2 (about 4.83), and write the results.
z-m-34-12.s.s2.hint.1: Divide the cases by the sizes of the distance and the radius in a table.
z-m-34-12.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I distinguish which formula to use when the distance is larger and when the radius is larger?
z-m-34-12.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is it clear which side I put the boundary (when the distance equals the radius) on?
z-m-34-12.s.s2.model.0: When the line and the circle do not meet, it is (distance from the center to the line) − radius, and if they meet or touch, the minimum is 0. If the distance is less than or equal to the radius, it is 0.
z-m-34-12.s.s2.model.1: Only when d is greater than r is it d − r, and if d ≤ r the minimum is 0.

z-m-34-13.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Harin's solution.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.hint.0: Put k = 2 and k = −2 into the two equations and write whether the lines they represent are the same or different.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which of the parallel lines and the coinciding lines the condition 'the slopes are equal' includes.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.line.0: If two lines are parallel, their slopes are equal.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.line.1: The slope of l₁ is −k/2 and the slope of l₂ is −2/k.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.line.2: From −k/2 = −2/k we get k² = 4, so k = 2 or k = −2.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.line.3: So the values of k for which the two lines are parallel are 2 and −2.
z-m-34-13.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. If k = 2, both equations become 2x + 2y = 4, which is the same line (coinciding). Under this task's convention, coinciding is not parallel, so the only parallel case is k = −2. (−2x + 2y = 4 and 2x − 2y = 4 are y = x + 2 and y = x − 2, different parallel lines.)
z-m-34-13.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different pairs (a, b) so that the lines ax + y = 1 and 4x + by = 2 are different parallel lines. (The values of a must be different from each other.)
z-m-34-13.s.s2.hint.0: Make the coefficients of y in the two equations the same, and then compare the coefficients of x and the constant terms.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.hint.1: After finding a pair with equal slopes, check whether one of the two equations is a constant multiple of the other.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.hint.2: Change a to 1, 4, −1 and so on, and fit b to match.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.ok.c1: The ratio of the coefficients fits, so the slopes are equal.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.fail.c1: The slopes are not equal. Write the slopes of the two lines in terms of a and b and make them equal.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.ok.c2: The two equations are not the same line.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.fail.c2: For this pair, the two equations are the same line (coinciding). A coinciding pair is not parallel.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.explain: If ab = 4 and a ≠ 2, they are different parallel lines. For example, (1, 4), (4, 1), (−1, −4), (8, 0.5). For (2, 2), the two equations are 2x + y = 1 and 4x + 2y = 2, the same line, so they are not parallel.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why there are pairs that satisfy ab = 4 but do not give parallel lines.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put a pair with ab = 4 into the two equations and check whether multiplying one side by a constant makes it the same as the other.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find which values of (a, b) give a constant multiple.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I check that the two equations in my example are really the same line?
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I explain the difference between 'parallel' and 'coinciding' in my own words?
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.model.0: If a = 2, b = 2, then l₁ is 2x + y = 1 and l₂ is 4x + 2y = 2, which is the same equation doubled, so it is the same line. Overlapping lines are not different parallel lines, so they must be left out.
z-m-34-13.s.s2.because.model.1: When a = 2, b = 2, the two lines overlap completely and coincide. Coinciding lines do not fail to meet; they meet at infinitely many points.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.prompt: Some textbooks also include 'two coinciding lines' in parallel. Following that definition, what are the values of k for which l₁: kx + 2y = 4 and l₂: 2x + ky = 4 are parallel?
z-m-34-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write whether the two equations are the same line when k = 2, and what happens under the definition that includes coinciding in parallel.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.hint.1: Draw what the two lines look like when k = 0.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.o.a: Only k = −2: the answer is the same whatever the definition
z-m-34-13.s.s3.r.a: If coinciding is also included in parallel, the case at k = 2 where they become the same line must also be counted as parallel.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.o.b: Only k = 2: at k = −2 the two lines meet
z-m-34-13.s.s3.r.b: Put k = −2 into the equations and check whether the two lines meet.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.o.c: Both k = 2 and k = −2: it depends on the definition
z-m-34-13.s.s3.o.d: k = 0 is included too: it has no slope, so they are parallel
z-m-34-13.s.s3.r.d: If k = 0, one line is horizontal and the other is vertical. Check whether the two lines meet each other.
z-m-34-13.s.s3.explain: If coinciding is included in parallel, then k = 2 and k = −2 are both parallel. Under the definition that leaves out coinciding, only k = −2. The same solution gives different answers depending on the convention, so you must check the definition in the problem.
